PullRequest.Title: launch: improve cross-platform setup and cleanup
PullRequest.Body: ## Summary - replace the Bash-only, `jq`-dependent Monaco paste implementation with a cross-platform Node helper - when authentication blocks launch automation, offer the user a choice between completing the current sign-in and bootstrapping the persistent source profile - keep persistent profile setup out of the normal launcher with small, dedicated Windows and macOS/Linux bootstrap scripts - add reliable Windows cleanup scoped to an isolated launch's exact user-data directory - document dependency-free JSON parsing and correct PowerShell forwarding of arguments after `--`

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The interval, synchronous subprocess call, all-process arguments (`ps -ax`/`ps -e`), and post-readiness lifecycle are explicit. Only the exact host process count and how long a user leaves the sign-in window open are uncertain, which affects magnitude rather than mechanism.
Findings.PerformanceResource: `ps` subprocesses plus CPU and allocations used to parse and rescan the complete process table
Findings.PerformanceScaling: Cost grows as 4 full scans per second × system process count × time the bootstrap window remains open; concurrent bootstrap windows multiply the rate.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: Sustained avoidable CPU/subprocess activity and reduced battery life while waiting for bootstrap sign-in
Findings.PreviousBehavior: Before this PR there was no bootstrap helper or detached process-tree monitor, so leaving a persistent Code OSS profile open did not create recurring `ps` subprocesses or full process-table parsing.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: The new detached bootstrap monitor schedules `check` every 250 ms; every check synchronously spawns `ps`, parses every system process, rebuilds PID sets, and walks the process list to extend the tracked tree.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: RIGHT line 110 newly installs a 250 ms interval around `check`; the same added block shows each invocation synchronously runs whole-system `ps`.
Findings.Title: Stop spawning `ps` four times per second for the bootstrap lifetime
Findings.Impact: During the documented flow the bootstrap script returns at CDP readiness and the user may spend minutes signing in before closing Code OSS. The monitor therefore launches about 240 `ps` processes per minute for each bootstrap window, causing avoidable CPU, subprocess, and battery load for the entire interaction.
Findings.Evidence: Added lines 57-110 launch a detached Node monitor. `check` at lines 68-103 calls `execFileSync("ps", psArgs)`, parses all rows, and scans them for descendants; line 110 repeats that work every 250 ms. SKILL.md lines 101-108 explicitly direct the caller to wait while the user signs in and only then close the application and consume the exit marker, proving the monitor remains live beyond startup.
Findings.Recommendation: Keep fast discovery only through initial CDP readiness, then switch to event-driven process tracking or a much slower idle cadence, returning to a short cadence only after a stop request. Preserve the exit marker and tree-cleanup semantics.

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The unfiltered CIM query, full-list scans, 250 ms loop, detached ownership, and post-readiness user-wait lifecycle are explicit. Machine process count and user sign-in duration only affect the size of the regression.
Findings.PerformanceResource: WMI/CIM IPC calls, full process objects, and CPU used to enumerate and rescan the system process table
Findings.PerformanceScaling: Cost grows as 4 full WMI enumerations per second × system process count × duration of the open bootstrap window; multiple bootstraps multiply it.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: Sustained avoidable CPU/IPC activity and reduced responsiveness or battery life during bootstrap sign-in
Findings.PreviousBehavior: Before this PR the Windows bootstrap and its monitor did not exist, so an open persistent Code OSS sign-in window incurred no recurring WMI/CIM process-table queries from this skill.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: The newly spawned hidden PowerShell monitor loops every 250 ms and executes an unfiltered `Get-CimInstance Win32_Process`, materializes the complete process list, and repeatedly scans it to discover descendants and liveness.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: RIGHT line 55 newly sets the loop cadence to 250 ms; the added loop body at lines 18-33 performs an unfiltered whole-system CIM query and repeated process-list scans each iteration.
Findings.Title: Avoid polling WMI for every process four times per second
Findings.Impact: The documented bootstrap flow leaves this hidden monitor running after readiness while a user signs in and closes the window. This causes about 240 full WMI process enumerations per minute, adding sustained CPU and WMI/IPC pressure throughout a potentially minutes-long interactive wait.
Findings.Evidence: bootstrap-profile.ps1 lines 73-75 starts this monitor detached before waiting for CDP and never stops it on success. In this file, lines 18-33 query and materialize all `Win32_Process` instances and scan them, while added line 55 repeats the loop after only 250 ms. SKILL.md lines 101-108 establish that the process remains open while awaiting user acknowledgement.
Findings.Recommendation: Track descendants with OS process/job or event mechanisms where possible. At minimum, use the 250 ms cadence only during initial startup/active shutdown and poll much less frequently after CDP readiness while preserving the exit-marker contract.

Scenarios.Scenario: Normal isolated launch with an existing or missing source profile
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Path resolution and source-profile checks precede profile preparation; when a profile exists, the existing copy/settings/prelaunch/app-start/CDP-ready chain remains. When it is missing, the diff skips source copy and auth preflight, creates an empty destination, then newly continues through Code OSS startup and waits for CDP instead of aborting.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Resolve the source path with `node -e` on macOS/Linux
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The shell validated and canonicalized only an existing source directory without starting Node here.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Adds one Node startup before profile preparation, but is constant and small relative to launching Electron.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Check/create/copy source and destination profile directories and update settings
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One source/destination group per launch; copy cardinality remains one grouped profile copy when a source exists and zero when absent.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Existing-profile launches already copied the profile and updated settings; missing profiles aborted before this boundary.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Profile preparation must finish before Code OSS starts. Missing-profile launches now create only the empty destination rather than failing.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Start Code OSS and wait for its local CDP endpoint
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One application process tree and one bounded readiness loop per launch
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: A missing profile caused immediate usage failure; existing profiles already incurred application startup and readiness waiting.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Launch output waits for readiness. This is newly reachable for a missing source profile, intentionally enabling sign-in; unchanged for an existing profile.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: One source profile and one destination per launch. Existing-profile cost scales with profile bytes as before; missing-profile launches copy no source files. The added Unix path normalization starts one Node process per launch.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Preparation and startup are serialized within each launcher. Separate isolated launches can run concurrently, as before; there is no added shared queue or burst beyond the intentionally newly reachable app launch for a missing profile.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: No new cache is added. Existing source-profile contents act as the seed; a missing profile is represented explicitly and skips auth/preflight and copy work. Repeated launches each prepare a fresh isolated directory.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: branches and boundary placement are explicit in both launchers.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: The startup cost newly reached by users without a profile varies by build and machine, but it is the requested workflow rather than avoidable duplicate work.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression. Existing-profile work is not amplified; missing-profile app startup is the intentional behavior, and source copy/preflight work is skipped.

Scenarios.Scenario: Bootstrap a persistent profile and wait while the user signs in on macOS, Linux, or Windows
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Bootstrap creates profile/log state, starts Code OSS, starts a detached tree monitor, and synchronously probes local CDP until ready. User sign-in occurs after bootstrap returns; the detached monitor remains off the immediate readiness critical path but consumes resources until Code OSS exits. After acknowledgement, `--wait-for-exit` polls the marker and blocks relaunch until cleanup completes.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One application process tree per bootstrap
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Required before readiness and user sign-in can proceed.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: At most roughly one local request per 100-300 ms for up to 90 seconds, stopping at readiness
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: No bootstrap path invoked the existing readiness helper.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Bootstrap JSON is withheld until readiness; this helper existed already but is newly reused by bootstrap.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Run whole-system `ps`, parse all rows, and rescan descendants
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Four subprocesses per second for the full bootstrap-window lifetime, about 240 per minute per bootstrap
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: No bootstrap monitor or recurring `ps` process existed.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Off the post-readiness interaction critical path, but remains as sustained background load and supplies the exit marker.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Query all `Win32_Process` instances over CIM/WMI and rescan descendants
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Four full CIM enumerations per second for the full bootstrap-window lifetime, about 240 per minute per bootstrap
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: No Windows bootstrap monitor or recurring CIM enumeration existed.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Off the post-readiness interaction critical path, but remains as sustained background load and supplies cleanup/exit tracking.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Create and poll stop/exit marker files and append logs
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One marker pair and log per bootstrap; wait mode checks the exit marker four times per second for at most 30 seconds
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Marker polling blocks only the explicit post-acknowledgement wait; otherwise it is small compared with process scans.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: One Code OSS process tree per bootstrap. The reported monitor cost scales with system process count, four scans per second, sign-in/window lifetime, and number of concurrent bootstrap windows.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Each bootstrap creates one independent detached monitor. Unix synchronously serializes `ps` calls inside each monitor; Windows serializes CIM queries inside each monitor. Concurrent bootstraps multiply aggregate scan rate without a shared limiter.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: There is no cache or coalescing for process-table snapshots. Every 250 ms scan refetches and rematerializes the complete table even when no process state changed. Persistent profile data may be warm across launches but does not reduce monitor work.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: Very high: detached ownership, 250 ms cadence, all-process queries, and documented post-readiness user wait are explicit.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Exact CPU/IPC cost depends on host process count and the time a user leaves the sign-in window open; the 4 Hz whole-system scan mechanism and unbounded-by-readiness lifetime are certain.
Scenarios.Verdict: Reportable on both implementations: two medium repeated-work findings were submitted for sustained whole-system process polling.

Scenarios.Scenario: Paste text into a Monaco chat input through Playwright
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The helper reads input, resolves the local Playwright CLI, sequentially focuses the editor, optionally sends select-all/delete, writes one temporary run-code file, executes browser-side paste/verification, parses output, and removes the temporary directory before returning.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Invoke the Playwright CLI for focus, key presses, and paste run-code
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Three calls with `--append`, four without; one logical paste per invocation
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The shell helper performed the same focus, optional two key presses, and one eval through `npx`; the diff replaces the wrapper with direct Node CLI launches rather than increasing call count.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: All calls are sequential and must complete before paste success is returned.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Create, write, and recursively remove one temporary directory containing `paste.js`
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One small directory and file per paste
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The old helper passed generated JavaScript directly to CLI eval and created no temporary file.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Synchronous and on the paste critical path, but bounded to one generated script; replaces passing the generated script through command arguments.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Embed input text into generated JavaScript and parse CLI result JSON
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One serialization and result parse per paste; output is bounded to verification metadata
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The shell implementation also JSON-escaped input and parsed a JSON result, using Node and jq.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Required for paste execution and status reporting.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: One invocation per paste. Subprocess cardinality is three CLI calls in append mode or four otherwise, matching the old helper. Serialization and browser verification scale with text size and rendered view-line count, with the same 20-attempt cap as before.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: CLI operations inside one invocation are synchronous and ordered. Separate named sessions can run concurrently as before; no new shared limiter or aggregate fan-out is introduced.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: `require.resolve` is memoized only within the short-lived helper process. There is no cross-invocation cache, but direct CLI resolution avoids the old `npx` wrapper startup on each CLI command. Verification has no cache and intentionally samples current DOM state.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: old and new command cardinality and verification loops are visible in the diff.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Temporary-file latency varies by filesystem, but it is one bounded file per user/agent paste and is offset by removing repeated `npx` wrapper resolution; no realistic regression mechanism is established.
Scenarios.Verdict: No finding. The helper preserves browser-operation cardinality and replaces heavier wrapper/JSON tooling; its new single temporary file is bounded.

Scenarios.Scenario: Clean up an isolated Windows launch
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Optionally close one Playwright session, enumerate matching Code OSS processes, force-stop them with bounded retries, verify none remain, then recursively delete one run directory with bounded retries.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Close one named Playwright CLI session through `npx`
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Zero or one invocation per cleanup
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Runs first so browser automation releases resources; failure is allowed to proceed to process cleanup.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Enumerate `Win32_Process`, parse matching command lines, and stop matching Code OSS processes
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Two queries when no process remains; up to six with termination retries
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Windows documentation had no exact-run cleanup helper; users cleaned up manually.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Cleanup waits for process release before deleting the run directory.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Recursively remove the isolated run directory
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One deletion, retried at most five times on failure
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: No scripted Windows run-directory deletion path existed.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Cleanup does not complete until deletion succeeds or retries are exhausted.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: One run directory and one optional session. Process enumeration is at least two and at most six whole-system CIM queries; directory deletion scales with files in that isolated run. All retry loops cap at five attempts.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Cleanup operations are serialized. It targets all matching Code OSS processes in each attempt but issues stops sequentially; there is no unbounded parallelism.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: No cache is used; process state is intentionally refreshed between termination attempts. Command-line parsing compiles the helper type once per PowerShell process and examines only Code OSS entries after the WMI query.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: query/deletion counts and retry bounds are explicit.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: CIM and recursive deletion duration depend on machine state and run-directory size, but invocation and retries are bounded and occur only during explicit cleanup.
Scenarios.Verdict: No finding. Although it performs whole-process enumeration, this is an explicit, bounded cleanup path rather than sustained or input-amplified work.

Analysis.Summary: Completed the performance pass over all 10 changed files and relevant call paths. Submitted two medium repeated-work findings for the new macOS/Linux and Windows bootstrap monitors, each of which scans the complete system process table four times per second for the entire user sign-in lifetime. Other changed launch, paste, and cleanup boundaries are intentional, bounded, or preserve prior operation cardinality.

Stats.CostNote: Copilot SDK reports nano-AI units and model billing multipliers; it does not provide a USD conversion.
